evals.query: Create a declarative Kora HTTP client UserApiClient for a User API: GET /users/{userId}, GET /users with page and size query params, POST /users returning the status code, and DELETE /users/{userId}. The base URL must come from configuration.
expected_behavior: Annotates the interface with io.koraframework.http.client.common.annotation.HttpClient and passes the config path as the annotation value, e.g. @HttpClient("httpClient.userApi")
Annotates each method with @HttpRoute(method = HttpMethod.GET/POST/DELETE, path = ...) imported from io.koraframework.http.common.annotation
Maps path variables with @Path and query parameters with @Query, marking optional ones @Nullable (Kotlin: T?)
Uses @Json on the method and on the body parameter, and adds implementation "io.koraframework:json-common" plus JsonModule on @KoraApp
Supplies the url key under httpClient.<client> in config and adds a transport module (OkHttpClientModule with io.koraframework:http-client-ok)
Uses the platform "io.koraframework:kora-bom" at 2.0.0.RC2 from mavenCentral() rather than pinning per-artifact versions
anti_behavior: Writes @HttpClient(configPath = "httpClient.userApi")
Writes @HttpClient(baseUrl = ...) or any baseUrl attribute
Imports ru.tinkoff.kora.http.client.common.annotation.HttpClient or any ru.tinkoff.kora package
Declares the BOM as ru.tinkoff.kora:kora-parent, or the artifact json-module
Returns CompletionStage, Mono or declares the Kotlin method suspend

evals.query: Our Kora 1.x client is declared as @HttpClient(configPath = "httpClient.userApi") and imports ru.tinkoff.kora.http.client.common.HttpClientResponseException. What are the Kora 2.0 equivalents?
expected_behavior: States that in 2.0 the annotation declares String value() default "" plus telemetryTag() and httpClientTag(), and there is no configPath attribute — write @HttpClient("httpClient.userApi")
States the annotation is io.koraframework.http.client.common.annotation.HttpClient
States the exceptions moved to io.koraframework.http.client.common.exception.{HttpClientResponseException, HttpClientDecoderException}
Mentions that HttpClientResponseException exposes getCode()/getHeaders()/getBytes() rather than code()
Notes the compile symptom of the stale attribute: cannot find symbol: method configPath()
Notes that omitting the value resolves httpClient.<lowerCamelInterfaceName> by default
anti_behavior: Claims configPath still works or is merely deprecated
Keeps e.code() as the accessor on HttpClientResponseException
Says the exceptions are still in ru.tinkoff.kora.http.client.common or io.koraframework.http.client.common (without .exception)

evals.query: Our Kora 1.x service depends on ru.tinkoff.kora:http-client-async and its @KoraApp extends AsyncHttpClientModule, with client methods returning CompletionStage. Migrate it to Kora 2.0.
expected_behavior: States that http-client-async and AsyncHttpClientModule do not exist in Kora 2.0 and there is no async transport replacement
Moves the dependency to io.koraframework:http-client-ok (or http-client-jdk / http-client-apache) and swaps the module interface accordingly
Rewrites every CompletionStage<T> client method to return T, because client contracts are synchronous and run on virtual threads

Explains that a leftover async return type produces the warning "Method has async signature, this might not work correctly" and then No component found for dependency: HttpClientResponseMapper<java.util.concurrent.CompletionStage<...>>
Moves httpClient.async config keys to the new transport section (httpClient.ok / .jdk / .apache)
Mentions removing io.projectreactor:reactor-core / kotlinx-coroutines once no usages remain
anti_behavior: Suggests io.koraframework:http-client-async or any AsyncHttpClientModule
Keeps CompletionStage, Mono or Flux as the client return type
Claims one of the remaining transports still supports async client contracts
Moves httpClient.async timeouts into httpClient.apache (or .ok / .jdk) instead of the shared httpClient block

expected_behavior: Removes suspend and declares fun get(@Path id: Long): Pet
Rewrites @HttpClient(configPath = ...) as @HttpClient("httpClient.petApi")
States that KSP rejects a suspend client method outright with "Suspend methods are not supported by the HTTP client generator"

Explicitly refuses to keep a default coroutine wrapper such as suspend fun get(id) = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { getBlocking(id) } inside the client interface, and explains that it is still a public coroutine API masking a synchronous contract
Notes that Dispatchers.IO is pointless overhead under virtual threads
Rewrites the calling chain synchronously and drops runBlocking / runTest and kotlinx-coroutines where no usages remain
If real parallelism is needed, points at Java StructuredTaskScope and warns it is a preview API whose shape must be re-derived from the JDK actually in use
anti_behavior: Keeps suspend on any @HttpRoute method
Adds a suspend default method delegating to a blocking one, with or without withContext(Dispatchers.IO)
Wraps the call in runBlocking inside the client interface
Suggests Dispatchers.IO to make the blocking call "safe"
Claims Kotlin coroutines are still a supported Kora HTTP client contract

evals.query: My Kora 2.0 client method HttpResponseEntity<Void> deleteUser(@Path String userId) fails the build with: No component found for dependency: HttpClientResponseMapper<java.lang.Void> (no tags). Fix it.
expected_behavior: Explains that the framework ships concrete response mappers only for String, byte[], ByteBuffer and HttpBodyInput, and that HttpResponseEntity<T> is a template factory needing a mapper for the payload T
Declares a @Component HttpClientResponseMapper<Void> (for example inside the client interface) that drains the body and returns null
States explicitly that the mapper must NOT be referenced with @Mapping
Explains the @Mapping trap: with @Mapping the mapper would have to produce the whole HttpResponseEntity<Void>, giving "incompatible types: Void cannot be converted to HttpResponseEntity<Void>"
Mentions that a plain void (Kotlin Unit) return needs no mapper at all
In Kotlin, declares override fun apply(response: HttpClientResponse): Void? with the nullable return type
anti_behavior: Adds @Mapping(VoidResponseMapper.class) on the deleteUser method
Suggests annotating the method with @Json to make the Void mapper resolve
Declares the Kotlin mapper as returning non-nullable Void
Claims the framework already provides an HttpClientResponseMapper<Void>

evals.query: In a Kora 2.0 HTTP client I have a @Mapping request-body mapper, a dependency-free response mapper referenced from @ResponseCodeMapper, and a response mapper that takes a JsonReader. Which of them need @Component, and why?
expected_behavior: States the rule is decided by how the generated client obtains the mapper, not by the annotation kind
A @Mapping request-body mapper (HttpClientRequestMapper) is always a constructor parameter, so @Component is always required

A response mapper named by @Mapping on a method or by @ResponseCodeMapper(mapper = ...) is instantiated by the generated code when the class is final (Kotlin: not open) with a single public no-arg constructor — then @Component is not needed
A response mapper with constructor dependencies such as JsonReader<T> cannot be instantiated by the generator and must be a @Component
Names the two symptoms: No component found for dependency when it is missing, Multiple components match when a self-instantiated mapper is also registered in the graph
Notes that @InterceptWith interceptor classes are always injected and therefore always need @Component
anti_behavior: Says every mapper always needs @Component
Says no mapper ever needs @Component
Recommends @Component on a dependency-free final @ResponseCodeMapper mapper without noting the duplicate-binding risk
Suggests registering the mapper via reflection, a service loader, or a Spring-style component scan

evals.query: Show me a Kora 2.0 HTTP client configuration that emits request metrics and logs for the usersApi client with a 10s request timeout, and explain how to verify the metric exists.
expected_behavior: Sets httpClient.usersApi.telemetry.metrics.enabled = true explicitly and states that metrics default to false in Kora 2.0
Sets telemetry.logging.enabled = true explicitly and states that logging also defaults to false (only tracing defaults to true)
Puts url and requestTimeout in the same per-client block
Mentions that a MeterRegistry must be in the graph (micrometer-module) or the metric is silently absent even when enabled
Names the client timer http.client.request.duration
Optionally shows a per-method override keyed by the client method name
anti_behavior: Claims metrics or logging are enabled by default in Kora 2.0
Uses the 1.x telemetry key pathTemplate instead of pathFull
Puts the per-client telemetry block under httpClient rather than under httpClient.<client>
Presents the configuration as complete without any MeterRegistry / micrometer dependency

expected_behavior: Changes the signature to HttpClientResponse processRequest(InterceptChain chain, HttpClientRequest request) throws Exception, with the chain as the first parameter
Removes the Kora Context parameter and explains that Context was removed from the framework, with no replacement
Calls chain.process(authorized) with a single argument
Keeps request.toBuilder().header(...).build() because HttpClientRequest is immutable
Registers the interceptor as a @Component and attaches it with @InterceptWith from io.koraframework.http.common.annotation
Reads the key from a @ConfigSource interface rather than a non-existent @ConfigValue annotation
anti_behavior: Keeps the Context parameter or introduces a substitute context object
Returns CompletionStage<HttpClientResponse>
Puts the chain after the request in the parameter list
Mutates the request in place instead of rebuilding it
Omits @Component on the interceptor
Imports ru.tinkoff.kora.http.common.annotation.InterceptWith

evals.query: Implement error handling in a Kora 2.0 UserService.getUser(id): map 404 to a not-found error and 5xx to service-unavailable, and handle a response body that cannot be decoded.
expected_behavior: Catches io.koraframework.http.client.common.exception.HttpClientResponseException and branches on e.getCode()
States that non-2xx throws HttpClientResponseException by default when no mapper claims the status
Handles decode failures by catching HttpClientDecoderException or the common supertype HttpClientException

States that the generated client wraps every response-mapper failure (JsonReader error, IOException, RuntimeException) in HttpClientDecoderException, so catching HttpClientDecoderException reliably covers an undecodable body
Offers HttpResponseEntity<T>, Either<T, E> or @ResponseCodeMapper as ways to avoid exceptions, and notes that only Either disables the status check

Mentions that HttpClientTimeoutException and HttpClientConnectionException are separate branches with no status code, and that a refused connection or elapsed connectTimeout is HttpClientConnectionException on OkHttp, JDK and Apache alike
anti_behavior: Uses e.code() instead of e.getCode()
Invents per-status exception classes such as NotFoundException or HttpStatusCodeException in the Kora API
Imports the exceptions from ru.tinkoff.kora.http.client.common or from io.koraframework.http.client.common without the .exception package
Claims HttpResponseEntity<T> alone stops non-2xx from throwing
Claims a decode failure can surface as HttpClientUnknownException or propagate as a raw JsonReader/RuntimeException
Treats a connect timeout as HttpClientTimeoutException

evals.query: In Kotlin with Kora 2.0, send a plain-text request body instead of JSON, and decode a different response shape for 200 versus every other status code.
expected_behavior: Implements HttpClientRequestMapper<T> with override fun apply(value: T): HttpBodyOutput returning HttpBody.plaintext(...) and references it with @Mapping(X::class)
Marks the request mapper @Component because @Mapping body mappers are always injected
Uses @ResponseCodeMapper(code = 200, mapper = X::class) and @ResponseCodeMapper(code = ResponseCodeMapper.DEFAULT, mapper = Y::class)
Implements HttpClientResponseMapper<T> reading response.body().asInputStream() and response.code()
Marks the response mappers @Component because they take a JsonReader dependency
Uses requireNotNull (or an explicit throw) around jsonReader.read(...) because JsonReader.read returns a nullable value in Kora 2.0
Imports @Mapping from io.koraframework.common.annotation.Mapping
anti_behavior: Uses the 1.x apply(Context, value) request-mapper signature
Treats jsonReader.read(...) as non-null in Kotlin
Imports Mapping from ru.tinkoff.kora.common.Mapping
Declares any client method suspend
Adds @Component to a dependency-free, non-open response mapper without warning about the duplicate binding

evals.query: Set up a Kora 2.0 HTTP client transport: 5s connect timeout, 30s read timeout, HTTP/2, an explicit proxy, and a per-client block for usersApi at http://users-service:8080 with a 10s requestTimeout. Which transport should I pick?
expected_behavior: Recommends io.koraframework:http-client-ok with OkHttpClientModule as the default choice
Puts connectTimeout, readTimeout, useEnvProxy and the proxy block at the base httpClient path, and followRedirects / httpVersion under httpClient.ok
Adds a separate httpClient.usersApi block with url and requestTimeout
Lists the three available transports (http-client-ok, http-client-jdk, http-client-apache) and their module interfaces and config sections

Notes that http-client-apache is new in Kora 2.0, reads timeouts and proxy from the shared httpClient block like the other transports, and keeps only followRedirects / maxRedirects / maxConnections under httpClient.apache
States that exactly one transport module may be plugged into @KoraApp
anti_behavior: Offers http-client-async or AsyncHttpClientModule as an option
Uses OkHttpConfigurer for advanced tuning instead of io.koraframework.common.Configurer<OkHttpClient.Builder>
Plugs two transport modules into the same @KoraApp
Repeats connectTimeout / readTimeout / proxy inside httpClient.apache as if they were Apache keys

evals.query: Make a Kora 2.0 HTTP client resilient: retry GETs, a circuit breaker on POSTs, a timeout, and a fallback that returns an empty list.
expected_behavior: Adds io.koraframework:resilient-kora and ResilientModule on @KoraApp
Declares typed specification interfaces annotated @RetrySpec / @CircuitBreakerSpec / @TimeoutSpec, each extending Retry / CircuitBreaker / Timeouter and pointing at a resilient.* config path
Annotates methods with @Retryable(Spec.class), @CircuitBreakable(Spec.class), @Timeout(Spec.class) — class arguments, not strings

Uses @Fallback(method = "...") without a value attribute, and places the annotated method and its fallback in the same class (a service class, not the @HttpClient interface, whose generated impl declares only the route methods)

Configures the circuit breaker with countBased.windowSize, and warns that omitting countBased fails graph init with IllegalArgumentException: CircuitBreaker 'X' property 'countBased' is not configured
Notes that named resilient sections no longer inherit from default
anti_behavior: Uses @Retry("name"), @CircuitBreaker("name") or @Timeout("name") with a string argument
Uses @Fallback(value = "name", method = "...")
Configures slidingWindowSize instead of countBased.windowSize
Declares the fallback as a default method on the @HttpClient interface
Marks the service class carrying the aspects final

evals.query: Our Kora 2.0 client httpClient.payments logs requests. Security found the partner's X-Signature header and the access_token field of the JSON token response in our logs. Our config has telemetry.logging { enabled = true, mask = "[hidden]", maskHeaders = ["X-Signature"] }. Fix it.
expected_behavior: Removes the mask key: it does not exist on the client (or per-method) logging config; the replacement text comes from a @Tag(HttpClientTelemetry.class) MaskingStrategy component
Restates the defaults in maskHeaders: ["authorization", "set-cookie", "cookie", "x-signature"], explaining that a configured list replaces the default one
Explains that headers are logged at DEBUG and bodies at TRACE on the client's .request / .response loggers

Adds a @Tag(HttpClientTelemetry.class) DataMasker, e.g. new JsonDataMasker(MaskingPathRules.builder().mask("access_token", new MaskingFull()).build()), which is applied to application/json and +json bodies

Notes that the tagged strategy and maskers are shared by all clients and that per-client body rules need a DefaultHttpClientBodyConverter subclass overriding selectRequestDataMasker / selectResponseDataMasker
Links or defers to kora-aop-logging for the shared DataMasker / MaskingPathRules model
anti_behavior: Keeps telemetry.logging.mask as a working key
Claims header names must be written in lower case for maskHeaders to match
Claims response bodies are masked by default or by maskHeaders
Invents an HTTP-client-specific masking annotation or config key such as maskBody

evals.query: We use the JDK transport (http-client-jdk) with httpClient.readTimeout = 10s. Does that bound our calls? And our Grafana dashboard groups http.client.request.duration by http.route but the series are gone after upgrading to Kora 2.0.0.RC2. Also, where are connection-refused errors logged?
expected_behavior: States the JDK transport applies httpClient.readTimeout as the per-request timeout when the client/method sets no requestTimeout, and requestTimeout overrides it
Says the client timer tags the route template as url.template (not http.route) and also carries server.port (80/443 when the URI has no port)
Says a failed call without a response is logged at WARN ('HttpClient error received') on the client's .response logger, so that logger's level controls it
anti_behavior: Claims the JDK transport ignores readTimeout or applies only connectTimeout
Tells the user to keep grouping client metrics by http.route
Claims connection errors are logged on the .request logger
